title: Genuina principia doctrinae de statu aequilibrii et motu corporum tam perfecte flesibilium quam elasticorum

deep.reconstruction:
Context: Euler is setting up the general equilibrium (and later motion) equations for a one-dimensional body (thread, rod, lamina) that is either perfectly flexible or elastic. He uses a cut: the portion AM is removed and replaced by forces at the cut point M that keep the remaining part BM in its state. On the previous page he argued that for a perfectly flexible thread the cut force must lie along the tangent MT. For an elastic thread the curvature at the neighbouring point m (measured by the elementary angle Tmt) requires an additional bending action.

This page, §VI: besides the tangential force along MT one must admit a force VP normal to the tangent. Euler pictures a rigid rod mT attached to the element mM, with a normal force VP applied to it at a point V. The unknown resultant of AM on M is thus reduced to two forces: one along the tangent MT, and one normal to it applied at a definite point V.

§VII: in modern notation,
- T is the tangential force, i.e. the axial force or tension N(s).
- V is the normal force, i.e. the transverse shear force Q(s).
- v = MV is the lever arm.

For a perfectly flexible thread V = 0 and v drops out. For an elastic thread the curvature at m demands a definite moment, fixed by the constitution of the spring ('ex indole elateris'). This moment must equal the moment of the normal force, Vv; since Mm is infinitesimal, the moment about m equals the moment about M to first order. So the product Vv is the bending moment M(s) = Vv, given constitutively (e.g. M = Ek/ρ, as in E065).

§VIII: these quantities are then carried to the adjacent point m as T+dT, V+dV, v+dv. On the next page they are balanced against the distributed loads p ds (tangential) and q ds (normal) acting on the element. This yields the classical planar rod equations: dT − V dφ + p ds = 0, dV + T dφ + q ds = 0, and d(Vv) = V ds (shear equals the derivative of moment), with Vv given by the elastic law.

In modern language, the cut action is a force-plus-couple (N, Q, M). Euler encodes it as a single force with components (T, V) applied at an offset v along the tangent.
errors: Not an error in the derivation, but a representational limitation. Encoding the couple as Vv with a finite offset v cannot represent a section carrying a bending moment but zero shear (pure bending, e.g. a rod under end couples, where Q = 0 and M ≠ 0). There v must go to infinity. So the force-at-offset picture is degenerate exactly where the moment is constant. Euler says V must vanish for a perfectly flexible thread, which is correct, but V = 0 does not imply zero moment. The moment Vv as an independent couple is the cleaner variable.
The identification of the moment about m with Vv (rather than V(v+ds)) is justified only to first order. Euler states this explicitly ('quoniam elementum Mm est euanescens'), so it is fine.

ideas.what: Cut principle for a 1-D body: replace the action of the removed part by forces applied at the cut
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (Truesdell credits E410 / Novi Comm. 15 with the general cut principle for rods)
ideas.where_published: E410 itself; discussed by Truesdell, Rational Mechanics of Flexible or Elastic Bodies 1638–1788 (Opera omnia II 11/2)

ideas.what: Decomposition of the internal action into a tangential force T and a normal force V, with V vanishing for perfectly flexible threads
ideas.modern_name: Axial force and transverse shear force in rod theory
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler 1771 (E410), per Truesdell; partial earlier hints in Jakob Bernoulli

ideas.what: Moment of the normal force, Vv, equals the bending moment required by the curvature (constitutive law of the 'elater')
ideas.modern_name: Bending moment–curvature relation (Euler–Bernoulli), with M = Vv
ideas.usually_credited_to: Jakob Bernoulli / Euler (E065, 1744; here combined with shear)

deep.surprise_reason: This is the well-known passage where Euler introduces the shear force into the general theory of elastic rods. It is extensively analysed by Truesdell (1960) and credited to Euler. The only minor point is the degeneracy of the force-at-offset representation in pure bending, which is a modelling remark rather than a missed result.
transcription_corrections: Transcription matches the image essentially; 'flexile' is as printed (title has 'flexibilium'). The heading on the page reads 'CORP. SIVE FLEXIBIL. SEV ELASTIC.'
